extracted.intended_audience: PCT applicants, IPEA examiners, national/regional patent examiners and patent attorneys
extracted.subtask_short: PCT novelty and inventive step examination
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing prior art, novelty and inventive step under the PCT when acting as ISA/IPEA (with EPO practice applied mutatis mutandis). Covers what counts as prior art, how to treat non-written and internet disclosures, translations, dates, and the problem-and-solution approach to inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written disclosure made available to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: A written description (document) should be regarded as made available to the public if, at the relevant date, it was possible for members of the public to gain knowledge of the content of the document and there was no bar of confidentiality restricting the use or dissemination of such knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: German utility models are publicly available as of entry in the Register even before bulletin announcement. See Rules 33.1(b) and 64.2. The standard of availability is actual possibility for the public to gain knowledge and absence of confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosures (prior art must enable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art disclosure is only part of the prior art if it enables the skilled person to practise the technical teaching which is the subject of the document, taking into account general knowledge at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied mutatis mutandis from EPO Guidelines G-IV,2. For chemical compounds merely naming a compound does not make it 'known' unless the document (with general knowledge) enables preparation/separation (or isolation for natural products).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date for novelty: filing or priority date
rubrics_metrics.description: For international preliminary examination all prior art publicly available before the international filing date or, where a priority is validly claimed, before the date of priority, is taken into account. Different claims or alternatives may have different effective dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty must be considered against each claim or part of a claim; prior art relevant to one claim may include matter with an earlier effective date that cannot be cited against another claim. If missing parts are furnished under Rule 20.5, the application date can be the date when Art.11(1) requirements are met unless priority/Rule 20.6 maintain the original filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of documents in a non‑official language
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant disputes the relevance of a document cited in the search stage that is in a non‑official language, and gives specific reasons, the examiner should consider obtaining a translation (or relevant part) and may send the translation to the applicant with the next communication in PCT Chapter II.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See GL/PCT-EPO B-X,9.1.2–9.1.3. The examiner should weigh the applicant's reasons and other prior art before deciding to pursue translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of machine translations
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may rely on a machine translation of a document in an unfamiliar non‑official language and should send it to the applicant; a translation must render the meaning in a familiar language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grammatical/syntactic errors that do not impede understanding do not prevent qualification as a translation. A general claim that machine translations 'cannot be trusted' is insufficient; the applicant bears the burden of adducing evidence (e.g., an improved translation) to show defects. If applicant substantiates objections, the examiner must take them into account similarly to disputes over publication date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art from other applications (Rule 64.3): 'content' definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the PCT, the prior art does not include content of other applications filed earlier but published on/after the relevant date; nevertheless such applications must be noted as they may become relevant under Article 54(3) EPC. The 'content' of an application means the whole disclosure—description, drawings and claims—including certain explicit disclaimers, allowable references and prior art explicitly described; it does not include any priority document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention must be drawn to such applications in the preliminary examination report (IPER). See GL/PCT-EPO B-XI,4.3 and GL/EPO F-III,8 for 'allowable reference' treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑written disclosure as prior art (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A non‑written disclosure (oral disclosure, use, exhibition or other means) is not part of the prior art for Art.33(2)/(3) unless the date of that non‑written disclosure is indicated in a written disclosure made available to the public on or after the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making available includes producing, offering, marketing, exploiting a product or applying a process, demonstrations, specialist training or television. For international preliminary examination, a non‑written disclosure is prior art only if its content is confirmed by a written disclosure made available earlier than the relevant date defined by Rule 64.1(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of non‑written disclosure (use, exhibition, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use may be constituted by producing, offering, marketing or otherwise exploiting a product, or offering/marketing a process or its application, or applying the process; other ways include demonstrations, specialist training courses or television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketing includes sale or exchange. Availability also includes future technological means of making aspects available. See Rules 33.1(b) and 64.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPEA determinations when prior use is alleged
rubrics_metrics.description: When the IPEA learns of an object or process used such that it may be prior art, it must determine (i) whether a written disclosure before the relevant date confirms the use; (ii) the date of alleged use; (iii) what exactly was used to determine degree of similarity with claimed subject‑matter; and (iv) all circumstances of use (place, form) to determine whether and to what extent it was made available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors such as demonstration details, delivery and sale can provide information on public availability. See GL/PCT‑EPO E‑II, ISPE 16.57 and PCT/AI section 801 for third‑party use.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle on availability by use
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject‑matter is made available to the public by use if, at the relevant date, it was possible for members of the public to gain knowledge of the subject‑matter and there was no bar of confidentiality restricting use or dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an unconditionally sold object gives the buyer unlimited possession of any knowledge obtainable from it; features discoverable by external examination are deemed available; but concealed features requiring dismantling/destruction are not. Extrinsic characteristics dependent on specific outside conditions (e.g., application to produce an effect) point beyond the product per se and are not considered made available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement on secrecy prevents public availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject‑matter has not been made available to the public by use or other means if there is an express or tacit agreement on secrecy which has not been broken, or if secrecy derives from a relationship of good faith or trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good faith/trust may arise in contractual or commercial relationships; confidentiality obligations bar public availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use on non‑public property generally not public
rubrics_metrics.description: Use on non‑public property (e.g., factories, barracks) is generally not considered public availability because employees and soldiers are usually bound to secrecy, except where objects/processes are exhibited, explained or shown to the public there, or specialists not bound to secrecy can recognise essential features externally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Does not include premises of a third party to whom an object was unconditionally sold or places where the public could see the object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility examples: when visitors make use public
rubrics_metrics.description: If visitors (e.g., customers, dealers) are allowed to see a press in a factory without an obligation of secrecy and the essential features are evident to observers, those visitors (not bound to secrecy) could communicate the information, making it publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given where dealers and clients could see a press and were not considered bound to secrecy; their ability to recognise essential features makes disclosure public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inaccessibility example: process not ascertainable
rubrics_metrics.description: If it cannot be clearly ascertained by exhaustive examination by which process a known product was produced, then making available of a process (as prior art) may be refuted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows importance of being able to demonstrate how an alleged use produced the claimed subject‑matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art by oral description
rubrics_metrics.description: If prior art was made public by oral description before the relevant date but a document reproducing that oral description was published only on/after the relevant date, the written opinion and IPER should draw attention to this non‑written disclosure as provided in Rule 70.9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non‑written disclosures must be flagged even if the reproducing document is later; see Rule 70.9 for procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet disclosures count as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures on the internet form part of the prior art; information disclosed online is considered publicly available as of the date it was publicly posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internet sites can contain highly relevant technical information including online manuals/tutorials. Establishing posting/publication date and burden of proof follows principles in the EPO Guidelines (G‑IV,7.5.1 etc.) mutatis mutandis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and preparatory documents treated per EPO practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards and standard preparatory documents are treated according to the principles laid down in the Guidelines for Examination in the EPO (GL/EPO G‑IV,7.6) applied mutatis mutandis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural and evidential rules for standards/documents preparation apply as for other written disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross references incorporate secondary teaching into primary
rubrics_metrics.description: If a primary document explicitly refers to a secondary document for more detailed information on certain features, the teaching of the secondary is to be regarded as incorporated into the primary if the secondary was available to the public on the publication date of the primary. The relevant date for novelty remains the date of the primary document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporation by reference only applies if secondary was publicly available by the primary's publication date; novelty date is still that of the primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors in prior art documents and obvious corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: If, using common general knowledge, the skilled person can see at once that a relevant prior‑art document contains errors and can identify the only possible correction, then the errors do not affect the document's relevance and the document can be considered to contain the correction when assessing patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two conditions: (i) immediate recognition of error by skilled person; (ii) identification of the only possible correction. Then correction may be read into the prior art for relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art for novelty: everything made available by written disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is novel if it is not anticipated by prior art; everything made available to the public anywhere in the world by written disclosure before the relevant date is prior art. Non‑written disclosures count only if a written disclosure before the relevant date confirms them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For novelty it is not permissible to combine separate items of prior art or separate embodiments in a single document unless specifically suggested. Matters explicitly disclaimed in a document (except disclaimers excluding unworkable embodiments) and prior art acknowledged and explicitly described are regarded as incorporated in the document. Dictionaries may be used to interpret special terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit features and direct & unambiguous derivability
rubrics_metrics.description: A document takes away novelty of any claimed subject‑matter derivable directly and unambiguously from that document, including features implicit to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: disclosure of rubber where elastic properties are clearly used takes away novelty of use of an elastic material. Limitation to 'derivable directly and unambiguously' is important; well‑known equivalents not disclosed are a matter for inventive step, not novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant date of a prior document for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior document should be read as it would have been by a person skilled in the art on the relevant date. The relevant date for written disclosures is as defined by Rule 64.1(b) (international filing date or valid earliest priority date); for non‑written disclosures see Rule 64.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If filing date of the application falls within two months after expiry of the priority period of the earlier application, the relevant date may also be the application date of that earlier application. Apply GL/ISPE 12.04 etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure requirement for novelty (specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject‑matter in a document is part of prior art only if the information given enables the skilled person, at the relevant date, to practise the technical teaching; a mere mention of a compound's name/formula does not make it known unless preparation/separation is enabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO applies option A12.02[1] of the ISPE Appendix. Consider general knowledge available at relevant date when assessing enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic disclosure vs specific examples
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic disclosure does not usually take away novelty of a specific example within that disclosure, but a specific disclosure does take away the novelty of a generic claim embracing that disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: disclosure of copper takes away novelty of 'metal' as generic, but not novelty of metals other than copper; disclosure of one of rivets takes away novelty of 'fastening means' generic but not other specific fastenings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit disclosure, parameters and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of novelty may be explicit or implicit where carrying out the teaching of the prior document inevitably results in the claimed subject‑matter. Examiner should only raise such an objection where there can be no reasonable doubt as to the practical effect of the prior teaching. For parameter differences, the burden of proof for alleged distinguishing features lies with the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant provides appropriate comparison tests showing differences, it may be questionable whether the application discloses all features essential to manufacture products with the claimed parameters (Art.5). No benefit of doubt if applicant does not supply evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of novelty: intended use and purity
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining novelty, non‑distinctive characteristics of an intended use should be disregarded. A known compound is not rendered novel merely because available with a different degree of purity if that purity can be achieved by conventional means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: substance X for use as a catalyst not novel over same substance known as a dye unless the use implies a distinguishing form (e.g., additives). Characteristics implied by use that distinguish forms must be taken into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of second or further medical use claims
rubrics_metrics.description: How novelty of second or further medical use claims is assessed depends on the IPEA; as EPO IPEA, the EPO examiner applies GL/EPO G‑VI,7.1 and subsections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatment of medical use claims differs by IPEA; see GL/PCT‑EPO B‑VIII,2.1 for EPO as ISA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of second non‑medical use claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim to the use of a known compound for a particular non‑medical purpose based on a technical effect will be interpreted as including that technical effect as a functional technical feature; novelty of such use cannot be deduced from a new property of the produced product—the use may be novel only if the process of production is novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a compound for production of a product is interpreted as a process claim; novelty requires novelty of the production process itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection inventions novelty assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection inventions (selection of elements, sub‑sets or sub‑ranges not explicitly mentioned within a larger known set) are assessed according to principles in GL/EPO G‑VI,8.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO examiner as IPEA applies GL/EPO G‑VI,8 and subsections when assessing novelty of selection inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of 'reach‑through' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that functionally define chemical compounds by their action on a biological target ('reach‑through' claims) may lack novelty because compounds falling within such a functional definition may already be known; applicant data sometimes demonstrates known compounds exert the action, establishing lack of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional definitions in terms of biological target do not necessarily confer novelty on compounds; applicant's own test results can establish that compounds meeting the functional definition are already in prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step: general requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention involves an inventive step if, having regard to the prior art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. The question of inventive step only arises if the invention is novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty and inventive step are distinct criteria. Refer Art.33(3) and GL/ISPE 13.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant prior art and dates for inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art for inventive step is as defined in Art.33(3); in determining what counts as prior art, the principles in GL/PCT‑EPO G‑IV apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply relevant date rules and consider documents cited in search report and other publicly available knowledge up to the relevant date (see GL/ISPE 13.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The person skilled in the art is presumed to be a skilled practitioner in the relevant field with average knowledge and ability, aware of common general knowledge at the relevant date, with access to prior art (including cited documents) and the means/capacity for routine work and experimentation normal for the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the problem points to another technical field, the specialist in that field is the skilled person. The skilled person is assumed to be in constant development in the technical field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common general knowledge of the skilled person
rubrics_metrics.description: Common general knowledge of the skilled person is applied as in EPO Guidelines (Section G‑VII,3.1) mutatis mutandis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construing documents for inventive step, take account of common general knowledge up to and including the day before the relevant date (Rule 65.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness test for inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: before the filing or priority date, having regard to the art known at the time, would it have been obvious to the person skilled in the art to arrive at something falling within the terms of the claim? If so, the claim lacks inventive step. 'Obvious' means following plainly or logically from prior art without exercise of skill beyond the skilled person's expected ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In considering inventive step, it is fair to construe any published document in light of knowledge up to the day before the relevant date and to have regard to all knowledge generally available to the skilled person up to that day. See GL/ISPE 13.11 and Rule 65.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem‑and‑solution approach (EPO standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO's problem‑and‑solution approach comprises three stages: (i) determine the 'closest prior art'; (ii) establish the 'objective technical problem' to be solved; (iii) consider whether, starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem, the claimed invention would have been obvious to the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this approach consistently; EPO uses option A13.08.1 of the ISPE Appendix. The approach aims to render inventive‑step assessment more objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The closest prior art is the single reference which discloses the combination of features that constitutes the most promising starting point for a development leading to the invention. It should be directed to a similar purpose/effect or belong to the same/closely related technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice choose the reference that corresponds to a similar use and requires minimum structural/functional modifications to arrive at the claimed invention. See GL‑VII,5.1 principles applied mutatis mutandis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulation of the objective technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish objectively the technical problem to be solved by studying the application (or patent), the closest prior art and the distinguishing features and the technical effect resulting from those distinguishing features, then formulate the technical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The objective technical problem may differ from the problem presented by the applicant and may require reformulation based on objectively established facts revealed in proceedings (e.g., search report prior art). Reformulation may make the problem less ambitious than originally presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Could/would approach for inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: In the third stage, the examiner asks whether there is any teaching in the prior art as a whole that would (not simply could) have prompted the skilled person, faced with the objective technical problem, to modify or adapt the closest prior art to arrive at what the invention achieves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between mere possibility ('could') and a motivation or teaching that would have led the skilled person ('would'). See GL‑VII,5.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims containing technical and non‑technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of claims comprising a mixture of technical and non‑technical features follows the EPO Guidelines (Section G‑VII,5.4) applied mutatis mutandis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulation of the objective technical problem when non‑technical features present follows GL‑VII,5.4.1; examples in GL‑VII,5.4.2 illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining pieces of prior art in problem‑solution approach
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible to combine disclosure of one or more documents, parts of documents or other pieces of prior art (e.g., public prior use or unwritten general technical knowledge) with the closest prior art when applying the problem‑solution approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If more than one disclosure must be combined to arrive at the claimed invention, that may indicate presence of an inventive step, especially if the claimed invention is not a mere aggregation. Apply Section G‑VII,6 mutatis mutandis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination vs juxtaposition/aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim consisting of a 'combination of features' should be considered as a whole; it is incorrect to argue that because individual features are known/obvious the whole is obvious. However, if the claim is merely an 'aggregation or juxtaposition of features' and not a true combination, showing that individual features are obvious may suffice to show lack of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish true synergistic combinations from mere aggregations; see GL/ISPE references (A13.08.8, A13.08.9) and GL/ISPE 13.12–13.14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'ex post facto' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware that once a new idea is formulated it can often be shown theoretically how it might have been arrived at; such hindsight ('ex post facto') should not be used to conclude lack of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention that at first sight appears obvious might still involve an inventive step. Do not retrospectively piece together motivations from later developments. See GL/ISPE 13.15.
